clinicalPearls: The pupils are small, usually bilateral and often irregular, and show light-near dissociation: they fail to constrict to light but constrict briskly to a near target
Pupils dilate poorly in the dark and respond poorly to mydriatic drops
Classically associated with tertiary neurosyphilis, historically the reason for prompting syphilis serology in any patient with these findings
The near response is preserved and brisk, in contrast to the slow tonic near response of the Adie pupil
The presumed lesion lies in the pretectal midbrain, sparing the near-reflex fibres while damaging the light-reflex pathway
Diabetes and other causes can produce a similar pupillary picture, so it is not entirely specific for syphilis
The finding should trigger a broader assessment for other features of neurosyphilis such as tabes dorsalis
reference.pathophysiology: The Argyll Robertson pupil is thought to arise from a lesion in the periaqueductal pretectal region of the rostral midbrain that interrupts the fibres mediating the pupillary light reflex while sparing the more ventrally located fibres subserving the near response. This anatomical separation produces the characteristic light-near dissociation, with small pupils reflecting associated damage to sympathetic supranuclear inhibitory pathways. The classic association is tertiary neurosyphilis, though similar findings occur with diabetes mellitus and other conditions affecting the same region.
additionalDifferentials: Adie tonic pupil with light-near dissociation
Bilateral small pupils from opioid or other drug effect
Chronic anterior uveitis with posterior synechiae
additionalInvestigations: Serological testing for syphilis (treponemal and non-treponemal assays)
Cerebrospinal fluid examination for neurosyphilis where indicated
Slit-lamp examination to exclude synechiae or iris pathology
Assessment for other neurosyphilitic signs such as posterior column loss
redFlags: Confirmed syphilis serology requiring evaluation and treatment for neurosyphilis
Associated dorsal column signs or lightning pains suggesting tabes dorsalis
Cognitive decline suggesting general paresis of neurosyphilis
New pupillary abnormality with other midbrain signs
reference.prognosis: The pupillary abnormality itself is fixed and does not recover, but recognising it allows diagnosis and treatment of neurosyphilis or another underlying condition, which alters the systemic prognosis.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the Adie pupil, which has a slow tonic rather than brisk near response and cholinergic supersensitivity
Failing to test the pupils at near and so missing the dissociation
Not ordering syphilis serology when the finding is identified
Overlooking anterior segment causes of pupillary irregularity such as synechiae
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the underlying neurosyphilis with parenteral benzylpenicillin as first-line therapy, using penicillin desensitisation where allergy exists
Confirm the diagnosis with treponemal and non-treponemal serology and cerebrospinal fluid examination to direct treatment
Screen for and manage other causes such as diabetes mellitus with glycaemic control where syphilis is excluded
Assess for and treat other manifestations of neurosyphilis such as tabes dorsalis and general paresis
Monitor treatment response with serial non-treponemal titres and clinical review, recognising the pupillary sign itself is fixed and will not reverse
Offer partner notification and screening for other sexually transmitted infections including HIV
Involve neurology, ophthalmology and genitourinary medicine as appropriate
